newsitem.title: FIJI: Fiji assembly to be suspended for constitution bid.
newsitem.headline: Fiji assembly to be suspended for constitution bid.

text.p: Fiji's parliament will be suspended for the first five months of 1997 to allow work on a new constitution to replace the current racially-biased constitution, a government official said on Wednesday
A joint parliamentary committee, chaired by the Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, will then present the new constitution to the South Pacific nation's parliament for debate.

"Unless there is urgent government business the parliament will suspend sittings from the end of December 1996 until May 1997 when it is projected that the committee's report will be tabled and debated," said the official.
Fiji's present constitution was introduced after a 1987 military coup, led by then military commander Rabuka, overthrew an Indian-dominated government.
Under the constitution indigenous Fijians are guaranteed a majority in the 70-seat parliament.
But an independent review of the constitution, sponsored by the government and released in September, called for an end to the political domination of indigenous Fijians.
The review called for 45 non-ethnic seats, 12 indigenous Fijian seats, 10 ethnic Indian seats and a handful of other minor ethnic seats in the 70-seat parliament.
The review also said that while Fiji's president should remain an indigenous Fijian, there was no reason to specify the ethnicity of the prime minister.

Rabuka, who said he staged the 1987 coup because native Fijians were losing control of their country, has welcomed the constitutional review and called for consensus in adopting a new, more balanced constitution.
But nationalists in Fiji are opposed to any change and some political analysts here say there is opposition within Rabuka's cabinet to the constitutional reform.
Indian Fijians make up about 46 percent of Fiji's 750,000 population. Indians were brought to Fiji at the turn of the century to work on the country's sugar cane plantations.
